requirements.requirement: On node1, /etc/cron.allow restricts cron scheduling to exactly root and opsadmin
requirements.summary: Baseline confirmed no cron.allow/cron.deny existed and opsadmin did not exist (cmd-97a26faa3e8a40f3). Executor created opsadmin, wrote /etc/cron.allow containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin' (root:root, 0644), and removed any stray cron.deny (cmd-277f88d872df42bd). Post-restart snapshot confirms the file persisted unchanged (cmd-8f6f813b43564c24).

requirements.requirement: Only root and opsadmin can actually schedule (install/list) cron jobs; other users are denied
requirements.summary: root and opsadmin successfully listed and installed a crontab entry, while a throwaway non-listed user (crontest) received 'You (crontest) are not allowed to use this program (crontab)' on both list and install attempts (cmd-277f88d872df42bd). A second independent ephemeral user (verifytest) was denied identically after restart (cmd-8f6f813b43564c24), reinforcing the result.

requirements.requirement: opsadmin exists as a usable account on node1 (implied by naming it an allowed cron user)
requirements.summary: opsadmin did not exist previously; executor created it with a home directory and locked password, verified id/crontab access before and after restart.

requirements.requirement: Independent node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id f9bf293d..., cron active, cron.allow contents, opsadmin present (cmd-c1f2c0009ce34831). Reboot acknowledged before disconnect (cmd-47a4b27c28c94cd9); connection reset then successful reconnect with new boot_id 72810ce8... confirmed an actual restart (cmd-8070961b414649b2, cmd-3c66ada1cbf744d3). Post-restart check shows cron service active, cron.allow intact, opsadmin functional, and enforcement still denying a new test user (cmd-8f6f813b43564c24). Consistent with the fixed global boot-identity observations changing from f9bf293d... to 72810ce8....

overall_summary: The executor fully satisfied the task: /etc/cron.allow on node1 now contains exactly root and opsadmin, opsadmin was created since it didn't previously exist, and enforcement was directly demonstrated (allowed users can use crontab, a non-listed user is explicitly denied). The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also completed with a clear pre-restart baseline, acknowledged reboot, boot-id change, and confirmed post-restart recovery of cron service, the cron.allow restriction, and the opsadmin account, consistent with the fixed global boot-identity snapshots. All test users created during verification were cleanly removed, leaving no residue.
limitations: No fixed lifecycle snapshot of /etc/cron.allow or user accounts is provided (only boot-identity, tmp, sockets, failed-services, package-health), so cron-specific state is corroborated only by executor-run commands rather than the independent collector.
A transient userdel failure (process still attached) occurred mid-sequence but was immediately corrected in the next command; not treated as a task or hygiene defect.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map directly to task fulfillment, verification, or the restart protocol, and were bounded/reverted. cmd-277f88d872df42bd created opsadmin (retained, required), created a throwaway crontest user for denial testing, installed then removed a test cron job for opsadmin, and attempted userdel crontest which failed transiently because a shell process was still attached (userdel: user crontest is currently used by process 1284) — this is not a hygiene defect, just a race that was immediately corrected. cmd-7db37a932bf1403e killed the lingering process and successfully removed crontest, leaving no residue. cmd-8f6f813b43564c24 created and fully removed an ephemeral verifytest user for post-restart verification. The reboot (cmd-47a4b27c28c94cd9) was a single, low-risk, evidence-bounded action tied to the restart protocol, not an unnecessary mutation. Lifecycle diff (after_executor vs after_prepare) shows only the expected boot-id-dependent /tmp systemd-private directories and boot-id-tagged socket listing lines — no unexpected residue, no failed services, no package-health regression.
